scenario: AITA for telling my dad I'm not sticking around? | My parents separated when I was pretty young and my mom was awarded full custody. My father wanted to stay in my life at first, but the courts ruled in favor of my mom controlling visitation until he found a place to live and got a job. He was really bad off back then, and my mom was at least able to make bills. Instead of getting his act together, my father never tried to get involved with me again until recently when my mom died and he accepted custody. He has a house, a job, a GF, and she has a little boy. All living together. I didn't have to move out of state or anything, but it's a good distance from where I've lived my whole life and my best friend was still willing to take the time and gas to come see me. When he got here, my dad was very standoffish and when he left I was told I wasn't allowed to interact at with him at all anymore. I'm sure it's because he's a year older, has face piercings and some tattoos, and does weird styles and colors with his hair. My dad went so far as to lock my social media so I can have no contact. But my best friend is like my *best friend.* We've been through a lot-we grew up poor, we've had our fair share of bullying and family problems. I love my mom, but she wasn't perfect and there was a lot of shit to work through. He is a great guy who's always stood by me, and my dad dismissed him solely on his appearance. I got pissed and told my dad not to expect me to be around in a year when I turn eighteen, and his girlfriend told me I should be ashamed for using that as blackmail. To me, if it's a choice between dad or best friend, I'm going with the guy who has been there with me the whole way. AITA for threatening to bail?

His best friend, who is a year older, still made the effort to visit him despite the distance. The dad even locked the person's social media to prevent contact. The person feels that the dad dismissed his best friend solely based on his appearance—face piercings, tattoos, and unusual hairstyles. First, the person's background: parents separated, mom had custody, dad wasn't involved initially. After mom's death, dad gained custody. Now, the dad is imposing strict rules, especially regarding the person's best friend. The friend has been a constant support through tough times, including poverty, bullying, and family issues. The dad seems to be making decisions based on the friend's appearance, which the person finds unfair.

The person's action: threatening to leave home when he turns 18 if he can't see his best friend. He's choosing his friend over his dad because the friend has been more supportive.

Now, considering morality. Is it wrong for the person to threaten to leave? Well, he's 17, about to turn 18, so he's almost an adult. His dad is controlling his social life, which is a big issue for a teenager. The friend has been a significant positive influence, helping him through tough times. The dad's reasons for cutting off the friend seem superficial—appearance-based. That's not a good reason to restrict someone's social interactions, especially when those interactions are positive and supportive.

The person is standing up for his right to maintain a healthy relationship with his best friend. He's expressing his frustration and setting a boundary. While the threat might seem like blackmail, it's more of a statement of his intentions. He's not actually doing anything harmful; he's just saying he won't stay if he can't have his friend around. That seems reasonable, especially considering the dad's controlling behavior.

On the other hand, the dad might feel he's protecting his son from negative influences, but the friend doesn't seem to be a bad influence. The person is choosing someone who has been there for him over a parent who is being controlling and distant. It's a tough situation, but the person's choice seems to be about maintaining his mental health and support system.

So, considering all this, I think the action is morally acceptable. The person is asserting his right to maintain a healthy relationship with his best friend, especially when his dad is being unreasonable. It's a tough choice, but it's about self-preservation and valuing the positive people in his life.
